title: New Technology for a Sharper Future
caption: The New Technology Telescope under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The New Technology Telescope, or NTT, sits between the arching Milky Way and the dark mountainside of ESO's La Silla Observatory. Since 1989 it has imaged the night sky in fine detail. Recent achievements include observing the merger of two neutron stars, studying the structure of asteroids, analyzing hundreds of planetary nebulae and researching planets around other stars.

Bigger mirrors collect more light, but they are harder to keep in perfect shape. Astronomers found that above five meters across, gravity bent mirrors enough to degrade images badly. The NTT, at 3.5 meters, was a pioneer meant to open the way to larger mirrors.

Its key feature is active optics, an idea from ESO engineer Raymond Wilson. A thin, flexible primary mirror sits on supports that push just enough to cancel the distortions caused by gravity. The approach was soon taken up at Keck Observatory in Hawai'i, on its two segmented 10-meter telescopes.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or color details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more starlight than the eye, so the Milky Way appears brighter here than it would to someone on the mountain.

explore: The source calls the NTT's design revolutionary and says it brought huge improvements to ground-based astronomy. Similar technology is still being developed today for some of the largest telescopes in the world.
